known.name: Head-specific sigmoid gate on SDPA output (Gated Attention, Qwen)
known.mechanism: Multiply each head's SDPA output elementwise by sigmoid(X·Wθ), computed from the layer input, before the output projection.
known.effect: Across 30 variants, this gate gave consistent gains over the baseline. It also improved training stability, tolerated larger learning rates, cut massive activations and attention sinks, and improved long-context extrapolation. A blog write-up reports first-token attention falling from 46.7% to 4.8%; that figure is not from the paper. Qwen3-Next uses this gate.

known.name: Sparse per-head attention gate on 12 residual channels (modded-nanoGPT speedrun)
known.mechanism: Each head's output gets a sigmoid gate fed only by the first 12 dimensions of the residual stream, which is a very cheap gate.
known.effect: Part of the speedrun record sequence that cut the world-record time by about 20%. The write-up says it speeds up updates and reduces BOS attention-sink behavior. No isolated number was found.

known.name: Value embeddings with per-head gate (speedrun and nanochat)
known.mechanism: Extra token embeddings are mixed into attention values, often on alternating layers. The nanochat variant gates them per head from the first 32 input channels with a 2·sigmoid range.
known.effect: Adopted as speedrun record 14 (4.41 min). No isolated loss delta found.

known.name: Long-short sliding-window attention pattern
known.mechanism: Alternate short-window and long-window layers, with window-size warmup and YaRN, instead of full context everywhere.
known.effect: Part of record 16 (3.80 min), together with a separate block mask. Gemma 3 uses 5:1 local-to-global with a 1024 window. A secondary summary says the ablation found only a slight perplexity cost.

known.name: Value Residual Learning (ResFormer / SVFormer)
known.mechanism: Add a residual path from the first layer's value vectors to the values of every later layer. SVFormer shares the first layer's values across all layers.
known.effect: Matches baseline validation loss with about 16% fewer parameters and about 20% less data. SVFormer roughly halves the KV cache at a small cost.
known.where: Language models of roughly 82M to 1.6B parameters

known.name: NormFormer HeadScale
known.mechanism: Scale each head's output by a learned scalar, initialized at 1, before the output projection. Combined with extra norms to balance gradient magnitudes between early and late layers.
known.effect: The paper reports better pretraining quality with negligible parameters. The stated aim is to shrink early-layer gradients and raise late-layer gradients.

known.name: Grouped low-rank output projection (DeepSeek-V4)
known.mechanism: Split head outputs into groups, project each group to a smaller intermediate dimension, then combine and project to the hidden size.
known.effect: Reduces the cost of projecting a huge concatenated head output to d_model. This is a cost saving, not a loss gain. Group counts come from secondary sources (e.g. 128 heads, 16 groups, 1024 intermediate).

known.name: MLA vs MHA vs GQA vs GTA/GLA at fixed query-head count
known.mechanism: Compare KV-sharing schemes (MHA, GQA-4, MQA, GTA, MLA, GLA) with FFN width and 12 query heads held fixed.
known.effect: MLA had the best average perplexity (40.80), ahead of MHA (41.94) and GQA-4 (44.16), but at 181M parameters versus 174M for GQA-4, so it is not parameter-matched.

known.name: Differential attention
known.mechanism: Subtract two softmax attention maps to cancel common-mode noise and sparsify attention.
known.effect: Original paper claims gains across sizes and token counts. A follow-up at 125M reports about +0.7% average downstream accuracy for DIFF, with the top-half-of-layers variant slightly better than all layers.

known.name: Talking-heads attention
known.mechanism: Learned linear mixing across the head dimension of the attention logits, before and after the softmax.
known.effect: Better masked-LM perplexity and better transfer to downstream tasks, with modest extra compute.

failed.name: Shrinking the QK dimension below head_dim 64
failed.why: A Pythia-160M ablation found severe degradation when the query-key dimension was reduced below 64, even at fixed parameter budget. Very small heads are a bottleneck, which argues against many smaller heads.

failed.name: Changing head count at fixed hidden size (PanGu-π Pro)
failed.why: The authors report that head count and head dimension (they use 128) do not noticeably affect speed or accuracy when hidden size is fixed. This suggests head-split tuning may be near-neutral.

failed.name: Aggressive KV sharing via GQA-4 at small scale
failed.why: At 188M, GQA-4 was clearly worse than MHA and MLA (average perplexity 44.16 versus 41.94 and 40.80). Plain KV-head reduction is not free, so it is a cost-saving move rather than a quality one.

open.direction: Test head-dimension sweeps (3×128, 12×32, 6×64) at 384 width with a latent-attention KV path. No controlled sweep for a latent-attention model of this size was found.
open.why: The evidence is mixed: tiny QK dimensions hurt, while 128 looks neutral or better. The penalty from small heads is said to shrink with model size, so results at 21M may not transfer.

open.direction: Combine a cheap sparse per-head gate on the SDPA output with the output projection, and check whether it removes the 10x layer-0 gradient imbalance.
open.why: The gate is known to reduce attention sinks and stabilize training, and HeadScale targets the early-layer gradient imbalance. Their interaction with QK-norm and four-stream residual mixing has not been reported.

open.direction: Per-layer heterogeneous windows with stochastic window sizes during training, rather than full context in every layer.
open.why: SWAX found that short windows mixed with global layers work best and that stochastic window sizing helps. That was tested with recurrent layers at 1.4B and 7B, not in a pure-attention small model.

open.direction: Grouped or low-rank output projection as a regularizer or capacity reallocation at small width, saving wo parameters for other uses.
open.why: DeepSeek-V4 uses it for efficiency at huge head counts. Nobody reported whether it costs or helps quality when the head output is only 384-dimensional.

open.direction: Apply differential or other noise-cancelling attention only to some layers (e.g. the top half), possibly paired with fewer, larger heads.
open.why: The 125M follow-up found the top-half-only variant slightly better than all layers, but it has not been tested with latent attention or at the 21M scale.
